feed.title: SHRINCS: 324-byte stateful post-quantum signatures with static backups

entry.title: SHRINCS: 324-byte stateful post-quantum signatures with static backups
entry.summary:
The security analysis of SHRINCS has been made publicly available through a [GitHub repository](https://github.com/SHRINCS/Security-Analysis), which includes three primary research papers. The main paper presents the full formal specification of SHRINCS alongside its EU-CMA (existential unforgeability under chosen-message attack) security proof. This proof methodically reduces the overall security of SHRINCS to the foundational properties of tweakable hash functions, message-digest functions, and pseudorandom functions (PRFs). Furthermore, the analysis provides concrete evaluations of security bounds for both classical and quantum adversaries.
In addition to the SHRINCS-specific analysis, two supplementary papers address broader cryptographic concerns that also impact other signature schemes such as SPHINCS+ and SLH-DSA. One details a classical bound for interleaved target subset resilience (ITSR), a key property of the message hash mechanism protecting FORS. The other paper establishes a new quadratic quantum bound for multi-target undetectability, specifically $4q^2/|M|$, improving upon previous linear bounds and enhancing understanding of quantum resistance in this context.
SHRINCS implements both a stateful component (FXMSS with WOTS+C) and a stateless fallback mechanism (SLH-DSA) unified under a single public key, both utilizing the same underlying hash function. This architectural decision necessitates a nuanced security proof that cannot simply treat the two components as independent. Instead, the security reduction explicitly links both paths, allowing each reduction to simulate the other. The resulting proof rigorously accounts for all possible configurations of the stateful tree, ensuring that the derived security bounds are robust across every scenario. Each step in the scheme is represented as an explicit game hop with precise quantification of security loss at every stage, and all theoretical bounds are instantiated with proposed concrete parameters.
Several notable findings emerged during this in-depth analysis. The examination critiques the tightness of the SPHINCS+ theorem from prior work, noting that while the security statement references the forger’s running time, the reductions assume construction of an entire virtual hypertree—a process requiring over $2^{72}$ hash computations for certain parameter sets, significantly impacting practical security estimates. This discrepancy is resolved through the introduction of a collection oracle, allowing for more accurate accounting and a restatement of the original SPHINCS+ bounds. Additionally, the analysis refines the treatment of reprogramming steps shared by both signature paths, providing sharper security bounds—gains of 34 bits classically for the stateless path and 33.4 bits for the complete scheme. For the recommended parameters, the classical security bounds range between 121.4 and 122.7 bits, evaluated via the query-counting approach, while quantum security bounds reach one at approximately $2^{58.0}$ to $2^{59.2}$ hash queries. These results depend on several conjectures: the validity of the SM-DSPR bound, the transferability of the collection-oracle lemma from ideal to concrete hash functions, and the assumption that the counter search in the WOTS+C signer always succeeds within its designated $2^{16}$ counters.
Peer review and scrutiny of these draft documents are actively encouraged, with feedback on statements, proofs, or quantitative figures welcomed either through issue submissions in the [repository](https://github.com/SHRINCS/Security-Analysis) or direct correspondence. There is also ongoing work towards a Lean 4 formalization of the three papers by Kev ([see pull request](https://github.com/SHRINCS/Security-Analysis/pull/1)), which remains a work in progress awaiting further review.
